readerTitle: Trust builds like interest and breaks like glass
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Ratners, 1991년 영국 보석 소매 체인) + 가상 사례 (온라인·매장 생활용품 소매, 부품 제조사)
insight: 평판은 한 번에 쌓이는 자산이 아니라 지킨 약속마다 다음 거래를 쉽게 만드는 복리다. 그래서 작은 약속 하나를 깨는 비용은 그 건의 손익이 아니라 앞으로의 모든 거래에 붙는다.
misconception: 평판은 오래 쌓았으니 한두 번 실수나 꼼수로는 크게 흔들리지 않는다. 지금 한 건 손해를 피하는 쪽이 이득이다.

sources.text: Gerald Ratner, speech to the Institute of Directors, London, April 1991 (widely reported in UK press)
Ratner, G. (2007). The Rise and Fall... and Rise Again. Capstone.
Signet Group company history (Ratners Group renamed Signet in 1993)

factChecks.note: Ratner의 연설 시점(1991년 4월, Institute of Directors)과 "total crap" 발언 인용을 1차 자료(당시 보도 또는 Ratner 자서전)로 확인하세요.
회사 가치 하락 규모는 흔히 '약 5억 파운드'로 인용되지만 출처마다 다릅니다. 카드에는 "hundreds of millions of pounds"로만 적었습니다.
Ratner의 퇴임(1992년)과 그룹명 변경(1993년 Signet)을 Signet 회사 연혁으로 확인하세요. 'one of Britain's biggest jewelry chains' 표현도 당시 규모 자료로 확인 필요.
소매·제조 판단 문제는 모두 가상 상황이며 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The jeweler who joked away his own company
body: In 1991, Gerald Ratner ran one of Britain's biggest jewelry chains. He had built it over years of cheap, cheerful gifts sold on busy high streets.
Then, at a business dinner, he joked that some of his products were "total crap." The joke made the papers. The shops never recovered.

image.label: A jewelry shop window with a crack spreading across the glass
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 반짝이는 반지와 목걸이가 진열된 보석 가게 쇼윈도에 한 점에서 금이 퍼져 나가는 장면. 실제 상호, 로고, 간판 문구는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The holiday orders are running late.
body: You run a homeware retailer with shops and a website. It's mid-December. Your warehouse is behind, and many web orders placed today will arrive after Christmas.
Your site still shows a banner: "Order now, arrives before Christmas." What do you do?

options.text: Keep the banner. Most orders will make it, and sales are strong
options.feedback: You keep this week's sales. But every late gift is a broken promise to someone who will remember it next December.

options.text: Show honest delivery dates and suggest picking up in store
options.feedback: You lose some web orders now. You keep your word, and the people who still buy learn your dates can be trusted.

options.text: Stop taking web orders until the warehouse catches up
options.feedback: No promise gets broken, but you turn away customers who would have happily bought with a later date.

cards.title: The rings didn't change. The meaning did.
body: After the speech, nothing in Ratners' shops got worse. What changed was what a Ratners gift said about the person giving it.
Customers stayed away. Sales fell, and the company's value dropped by hundreds of millions of pounds. Ratner left in 1992, and the group dropped his name soon after.
Years of steady trust had worked like savings. **One sentence withdrew them.**

cards.title: Reputation compounds
body: **Reputation** is what people expect from you, based on how you kept your promises before.
It **compounds**: each kept promise makes the next deal a little easier. Returning customers need less persuading. They bring friends. Suppliers give better terms. People forgive an honest mistake.
Those gains build on each other, like interest on savings. A business that keeps its word for ten years isn't ten times better off than after one year. It's far more.

image.label: A stack of coins growing taller, each coin labeled 'kept promise'
image.brief: 동전 탑이 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 점점 빠르게 높아지는 인포그래픽. 동전마다 "Kept promise" 라벨. 위쪽에 작은 아이콘들(재방문, 추천, 좋은 거래 조건)이 동전 탑에서 뻗어 나옴.

cards.title: Where the interest comes from
body: Trust lowers the cost of almost everything a business does:
list: **Selling:** fewer ads and discounts needed to win a sale
**Word of mouth:** happy customers do part of the marketing
**Partners:** suppliers and lenders ask fewer questions
**Hiring:** good people want to work somewhere respected
**Mistakes:** a trusted business gets the benefit of the doubt
cards.callout: Each kept promise makes the next promise cheaper to keep and easier to believe.

cards.title: Compounding runs faster backwards.
body: Ratner's chain took years to build and days to break. That gap is normal. People notice and repeat bad news more than good news, and one broken promise makes them doubt all the earlier ones.
So a shortcut doesn't cost only the one sale it touches. It puts a question mark on every future sale.
cards.softwareNote: In software, reputation lives in reviews, ratings and how you handle outages. Users tolerate a bug that's fixed openly. A hidden data problem, once found, can undo years of good ratings.

cards.title: Don't let fear freeze you.
body: Guarding your reputation doesn't mean never making mistakes. Mistakes handled quickly and honestly often add to trust.
Reputation is also narrow. Being known for fast delivery doesn't make people trust your new product line.
And compounding needs memory. It pays most where customers and partners come back. In a one-off market, its pull is weaker, though word still travels.

cards.title: Now it's a parts factory.
body: You make metal brackets for a furniture maker that has bought from you for years. You find that last month's shipment has a slightly weak weld. They haven't noticed, and most brackets will probably be fine.
What do you do?

options.text: Fix the process quietly and say nothing about last month
options.feedback: You avoid an awkward call and a replacement bill. But if the weak brackets fail later, the hidden part costs far more trust than the defect.

options.text: Call them now, explain, and replace the batch at your cost
options.feedback: It costs money this month. It also proves that your word holds even when hiding would be easy, which is what keeps them buying from you.

options.text: Wait and handle it only if they complain
options.feedback: You save money if nothing happens. If something does, they learn you knew and stayed silent.

cards.title: Every promise is a deposit or a withdrawal.
body: Reputation grows slowly by building on itself, and falls fast. Judge a shortcut by what it does to every future deal, not just this one.
**Try it today:** list the promises your business makes out loud, like delivery dates, quality and returns. Circle the one you keep least reliably.
